questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes monitoring from observability, using the 'known unknown / unknown unknown' framing from Chapter 1?
options: Monitoring answers known unknowns by watching predefined signals against set thresholds; observability answers unknown unknowns by letting you investigate novel problems from data already being emitted
Monitoring and observability are two names for the same practice; the terms are interchangeable in modern tooling
Observability answers known unknowns because it requires you to predefine every dashboard in advance, while monitoring handles anything unexpected
Monitoring is only used in cloud environments, while observability is exclusive to on-premises infrastructure
Observability simply means collecting more metrics than monitoring does; the difference is purely a matter of data volume
Monitoring requires a dedicated query language, while observability only ever uses pre-built dashboards
questions.explain: Monitoring is built around known unknowns: predefined signals compared against thresholds you set in advance. Observability is a property that lets you investigate unknown unknowns -- failure modes nobody anticipated -- by slicing and correlating data you already have, without shipping new instrumentation first.
questions.distractorExplain: Treating the difference as just 'how much data you collect' misses the actual distinction. A system can emit a huge volume of metrics and still only answer the questions someone thought to ask in advance -- that's monitoring, however much data it involves. Observability is about whether you can answer a question nobody predefined a check for, not about volume.

questions.prompt: Match each of the three pillars' building blocks to what it actually is, per Lesson 2.
right: A timestamped, immutable record of one discrete event with rich detail
One timed segment of a trace, representing work done in one service or operation
A numeric measurement sampled over time, cheap to store and fast to query
The end-to-end path of one request across services, broken into timed segments
questions.explain: A metric is a numeric measurement sampled over time -- cheap and fast, good for dashboards and alerts. A log is a timestamped record of one discrete event with rich detail. A trace is the end-to-end path of one request across every service it touches. A span is one timed segment within that trace.

questions.prompt: Northbridge's checkout SLO is 99.9% success over a rolling 30-day window. Expressed as a percentage, how big is the error budget?
questions.explain: An error budget is the SLO flipped into a spending allowance: 100% minus the SLO. If the SLO is 99.9% success, the error budget is the remaining 0.1% -- the amount of failure the team is explicitly allowed before breaching the objective.

questions.prompt: Select every one of Google SRE's four golden signals, per Lesson 4.
options: Latency
Traffic
Errors
Saturation
Throughput
Availability
questions.explain: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. Throughput and availability are related operational concepts, but they aren't the four signals Lesson 4 names -- saturation in particular is the one teams most often skip even though it's frequently the earliest warning sign.

questions.prompt: Northbridge pages an on-call engineer because disk usage on a checkout pod is at 60%, and there is no action they can take right now. Per the alerting philosophy in Lesson 5, what's the correct take on this alert?
options: It should not page a human at all -- it fails the actionable test, since there's nothing the engineer can do immediately; a dashboard or non-urgent ticket is the right output
It's a well-designed alert, because any resource crossing 50% utilization should always notify on-call immediately
It should page the on-call engineer immediately, but at a lower severity than a checkout outage
It should be converted into a cause-based alert on CPU instead, since cause-based alerts are always preferable to symptom-based ones
questions.explain: Every alert must pass the actionable test: if a human is paged, is there something they can do right now? Paging someone for 60% disk usage with no immediate action available trains them to ignore pages -- the right output is a dashboard or a non-urgent ticket, not a 2 a.m. page.

questions.prompt: Northbridge's checkout service throws an unhandled exception with a full stack trace. Which Azure Monitor store does that exception actually land in, and why?
options: Azure Monitor Logs, in a Log Analytics workspace -- exceptions are structured/free-text records with rich detail, which is what Logs, not Metrics, are built to store
Azure Monitor Metrics, because every platform metric is collected automatically with no configuration
Metrics Explorer, because it's the fastest way to chart any data Azure collects
Neither -- exceptions aren't retained by Azure Monitor at all
questions.explain: Azure Monitor keeps two separate stores for a reason: Metrics are lightweight numerical time series (CPU percentage, request count), while Logs are structured or free-text records -- a line in a web server log, an exception with its full stack trace -- stored in a Log Analytics workspace and queried with KQL.

questions.code:
AppRequests
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize AvgDuration = avg(DurationMs) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
questions.prompt: In the KQL query above, what is the name of the operator written as a single vertical bar that chains each line into the next, passing one operator's output as the next one's input?
questions.explain: KQL reads left to right: you start with a table, then pipe (|) its rows through a chain of operators that each narrow or reshape the data. Each operator's output becomes the next operator's input.

questions.prompt: Match each part of an Azure Monitor alert rule to what it actually controls, per Lesson 9.
right: A Sev 0-4 ranking that shapes how an alert is sorted and triaged in the Alerts list
The data source an alert watches -- a metric, a log query, or an activity log event
A reusable, named bundle of notifications and actions attachable to many alert rules
The threshold logic applied to the signal that determines when the alert fires
questions.explain: An alert rule's signal is the data source (metric, log query, or activity log event); its condition is the threshold logic applied to that signal; its action group is the reusable bundle of notifications that fires when the condition is met; and severity is the Sev 0-4 ranking that shapes triage, independent of whether the alert fires.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of creating an Azure Monitor alert rule, per Lesson 9, in the correct order.
items: Pick the signal -- a metric, log query, or activity log event -- for the resource to watch
Define the condition's threshold logic, such as average response time over 2 seconds for 3 consecutive periods
Attach an action group -- the bundle of notifications and actions that fires when the condition is met
Set the severity level so the alert sorts correctly in the Alerts list for triage
questions.explain: Every Azure Monitor alert rule starts with picking the signal, then shaping the condition's threshold logic, then attaching a reusable action group, with severity set so the alert triages correctly alongside every other alert in the list.

questions.prompt: A team creates a new CloudWatch alarm on the checkout load balancer's TargetResponseTime two minutes ago. What state is the alarm most likely in right now, and why?
options: INSUFFICIENT_DATA -- the alarm hasn't collected enough data points yet to evaluate the condition
ALARM -- any newly created alarm defaults to the breached state until proven otherwise
OK -- CloudWatch always initializes new alarms as healthy regardless of data
The alarm has no state until it is manually acknowledged in the console
questions.explain: A CloudWatch alarm is always in one of three states: OK, ALARM, or INSUFFICIENT_DATA. A newly created alarm commonly sits in INSUFFICIENT_DATA because it hasn't yet collected enough data points to evaluate -- that's normal, not a sign anything is broken.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about AWS CloudTrail, per Lesson 13.
options: Event history logs the last 90 days of management events automatically, with no configuration required
Data events, like an S3 GetObject call, are logged by default alongside management events
A trail can deliver events to an S3 bucket for retention beyond 90 days and across every region in the account
CloudTrail Insights analyzes management event patterns and flags statistically unusual activity automatically
CloudTrail must be manually enabled on an AWS account before it starts recording any events
questions.explain: CloudTrail is on for every AWS account automatically, logging 90 days of management events into Event history with zero setup -- data events are higher-volume and off by default, requiring explicit enabling. A trail extends retention beyond 90 days and can span every region. CloudTrail Insights flags unusual activity automatically, without anyone writing a detection rule.

questions.prompt: In AWS X-Ray, one service's record of the work it did for a request -- with a start time, end time, and metadata, and which can contain finer-grained subsegments -- is called a ____.
questions.explain: Each service a request passes through records a segment: a record of the work that service did, with a start time, end time, and metadata. A segment can contain subsegments for finer detail, and segments stitched together across every service form one trace.

questions.prompt: Match each AWS monitoring tool to what it actually does, per Chapter 3.
right: Records every API call made against the AWS account, by anyone or anything
Compares a metric against a static or learned threshold and moves between OK, ALARM, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA
A purpose-built query language for interactively searching and aggregating log data
Distributed tracing that follows one request across every service boundary it crosses
questions.explain: CloudWatch Alarms compare a metric against a threshold and move between OK, ALARM, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA. CloudWatch Logs Insights is the purpose-built query language for searching log data. X-Ray is distributed tracing across service boundaries. CloudTrail records every API call made against the account.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how Prometheus collects metrics, per Chapter 4?
options: Prometheus pulls metrics by making an HTTP GET request against a /metrics endpoint on a schedule, typically every 15-30 seconds
Applications push their metrics to the Prometheus server over a message queue, and Prometheus stores whatever arrives
Prometheus requires every application to write directly into its TSDB using a proprietary binary protocol
Metrics are pulled only once, at application startup, and never refreshed afterward
Prometheus always pushes metrics to applications, which then forward them to Grafana for storage
The Pushgateway is how every application, long-running or not, is expected to send Prometheus its metrics
questions.explain: Prometheus flips the usual push model around: the Prometheus server scrapes (pulls) metrics from applications on a schedule, typically every 15-30 seconds, by making an HTTP GET request to a /metrics endpoint each application exposes.
questions.distractorExplain: The Pushgateway is real, but it's explicitly the exception, not the rule -- it exists only for short-lived batch jobs that would finish and exit before Prometheus's next scheduled scrape could ever catch them. Any long-running service, like Northbridge's checkout service, is instrumented for Prometheus to pull directly, never routed through the Pushgateway.

questions.prompt: A dashboard panel graphs this counter's raw value directly, without wrapping it in rate(). What does the resulting graph look like, and why?
options: A staircase that only ever climbs upward, because a counter never decreases except on a process restart -- which is exactly why you almost never graph a counter's raw value directly
A smooth line oscillating up and down in direct proportion to actual request volume
A flat, constant line, because Prometheus automatically normalizes counters before display
An error, because counters can't be queried or graphed without wrapping them in rate() first
questions.explain: A counter is cumulative and only ever increases (or resets to zero on a restart). Graphed raw, it's a staircase that only climbs -- useless on its own, which is exactly why rate() exists: to turn that climbing counter into a meaningful per-second rate.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the PromQL function used in the query above, which estimates a percentile from a histogram metric's bucket counts?
questions.explain: histogram_quantile() estimates a percentile from a histogram's bucket counts -- in this example, the 95th-percentile checkout duration over the last 5 minutes.

questions.prompt: Select every one of the four Prometheus client-library metric types covered in Lesson 15.
options: Counter
Gauge
Histogram
Summary
Timer
Delta
questions.explain: Prometheus's client libraries give you four metric types: counter (only ever increases), gauge (goes up and down), histogram (buckets observations for percentiles), and summary (client-side percentiles, not aggregatable across instances). 'Timer' and 'Delta' are not Prometheus metric types.

questions.prompt: Match each Prometheus/Grafana term to what it actually does, per Chapter 4.
right: The separate process that groups, deduplicates, silences, and routes firing alerts
Rules that keep, drop, or rewrite a discovered target's labels before Prometheus scrapes it
A small HTTP server that translates a system's native metrics into Prometheus's exposition format
Continuously asking a source like the Kubernetes API what targets should currently be scraped
questions.explain: An exporter translates a system's native metrics into Prometheus's format. Service discovery continuously asks a source like the Kubernetes API what to scrape. Relabeling rules keep, drop, or rewrite discovered labels before the scrape happens. Alertmanager groups, deduplicates, silences, and routes firing alerts.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a Prometheus alert reaching a human, per Lesson 19, in the correct order.
items: An alerting rule combining a PromQL expression and a 'for' duration is defined on the Prometheus server
The condition stays true for the full 'for' duration, so the alert moves to firing and appears on Prometheus's own Alerts page
Prometheus pushes the firing alert, with its label set, on to Alertmanager
Alertmanager groups and deduplicates matching alerts, then routes the notification to the correct receiver
questions.explain: An alerting rule lives on the Prometheus server, not Alertmanager. Once its condition holds true for the full 'for' duration, it fires and shows on Prometheus's Alerts page, then gets pushed to Alertmanager, which groups, deduplicates, and routes it to the right receiver -- Slack, PagerDuty, or similar.

questions.prompt: Northbridge's checkout request touches the checkout, inventory, and payment services, each logging independently in structured JSON. Without any further tooling, what's the most reliable way to reconstruct every log line that belongs to that one request, per Lesson 20?
options: Search every service's log index for the shared correlation_id value that was generated once at the edge and propagated through every downstream call
Sort all logs by timestamp across every service and assume lines that land close together belong to the same request
Filter every log index to level:error, since only error-level lines matter during an incident
There's no reliable way to do this without switching to a single monolithic service
questions.explain: A correlation ID is generated once, at the edge of the system, and passed through every downstream call, included in every log line any service writes while handling that request. Searching any log index for that shared value reconstructs the full story across every service that touched the request, in order.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Grafana Loki, as contrasted with the ELK stack in Lesson 21.
options: Loki indexes only a small set of labels, not the full text of every log line
Loki's query language, LogQL, is modeled on PromQL
Loki is generally more expensive to run at scale than Elasticsearch, because it builds a full-text index
LogQL can produce metric-style queries directly over logs, such as a rate() over matching log lines
Kibana is Loki's web UI for searching and visualizing indexed data
questions.explain: Loki indexes only labels, not full log text, storing raw text in cheap compressed chunks -- which is why it's cheaper at scale than Elasticsearch, not more expensive. LogQL is modeled on PromQL and supports metric-style queries over logs. Kibana is Elasticsearch's UI; Loki is queried through Grafana's own Explore view.

questions.prompt: In OpenTelemetry, a trace is the full tree of what, created while handling one request and linked together by a shared trace ID?
questions.explain: A span represents one unit of work with a start time, duration, and attributes. A trace is the full tree of spans created while handling one request, linked by a shared trace ID, with each span pointing to its parent span.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of correlating the three pillars during Northbridge's flash-sale incident, per Lesson 23, in the correct order.
items: A metric alert fires, showing checkout p99 latency climbing past the SLO -- confirming something is wrong and roughly when
Filtering logs to the alert's timestamp surfaces a cluster of error lines carrying a trace_id field
Opening that trace_id in a tracing backend's waterfall view shows exactly which span the time was actually spent in
questions.explain: The realistic investigation order moves from metric to log to trace: the metric says something is wrong and roughly when, the logs narrow down the what using a shared trace_id, and the trace shows exactly where the time went.

questions.prompt: Northbridge's inventory-service database connection pool is at 60% utilization, but requests are queued waiting for a connection. Applying the USE method from Lesson 24, how should this resource be classified?
options: Saturated -- a long wait queue means it's a bottleneck even though it isn't fully utilized yet
Healthy -- anything under 80% utilization can't be the bottleneck
Erroring -- a wait queue always indicates the resource is actively failing requests
Under-provisioned in Utilization terms only; saturation doesn't apply to connection pools
questions.explain: The USE method asks Utilization, Saturation, and Errors of a resource separately. A resource can be under-utilized and still be the bottleneck if saturation is high -- a connection pool at 60% utilization with a long wait queue is saturated, not fine.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the SEV1-SEV4 severity scale from Lesson 25.
options: A SEV1 incident requires an incident commander and typically pages all hands immediately
Severity determines who gets paged, whether a status page update goes out, and whether an incident commander is assigned
SEV4 means no customer impact, and it's logged for later review rather than triggering an immediate response
Once an incident is classified as a SEV1, its severity can never be changed for the rest of the incident
The incident commander's job is to personally fix the technical problem, not to coordinate the response
questions.explain: SEV1 pages all hands with a required incident commander. Severity determines paging, status page updates, and whether a commander is assigned. SEV4 has no customer impact and is simply logged. Severity can be changed as understanding of impact improves, and the incident commander coordinates the response rather than doing the hands-on fix.

questions.prompt: The four parts every good runbook needs, per Lesson 26, are trigger condition, diagnostic steps, remediation steps, and ____.
questions.explain: A runbook's four parts are the trigger condition, diagnostic steps, remediation steps, and an escalation path -- who to page and when, if remediation doesn't resolve it or the diagnosis doesn't match any known cause.

questions.prompt: Match each incident-response term to what it actually is, per Chapter 6.
right: A document assuming everyone acted reasonably given what they knew, focused on fixing the system rather than the person
Scheduled responsibility for responding to pages, rotated across a team
The person coordinating an incident response, distinct from whoever is actively fixing the issue
Defined steps for re-paging when an alert goes unacknowledged within a set window
questions.explain: An on-call rotation assigns scheduled paging responsibility. An escalation policy defines re-paging steps when an alert goes unacknowledged. The incident commander coordinates the response, separate from the person fixing the issue. A blameless postmortem assumes everyone acted reasonably and focuses on the system, not the person.

questions.prompt: In Northbridge's checkout postmortem, the undersized, never-load-tested database connection pool is named the root cause. What role does the missing early-warning alert on pool saturation play, per Lesson 27?
options: A contributing factor -- it made the incident harder to catch early, even though it didn't directly cause the pool to saturate
A second root cause, since a postmortem can never have more than one contributing factor
An action item, because action items are always defined before the incident happens
Irrelevant to the postmortem, since only the root cause needs to be documented
questions.explain: A contributing factor is a condition that made the incident worse or harder to catch, even without directly causing it. The missing saturation alert didn't cause the pool to fill up, but it meant the team only found out once the pool was already exhausted -- that's exactly the role of a contributing factor, distinct from the root cause.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building the capstone, per Lesson 30, in the correct order.
items: Instrument metrics with a client library, exposing a request counter, a duration histogram, and one saturation metric
Switch logs to structured JSON, including a correlation ID on every request or job-run log line
Wrap the call to your one dependency in a basic trace span
Build a 4-6 panel dashboard covering request rate, latency, error rate, and saturation
Write 2-3 symptom-based alert rules against real thresholds observed from the running service
questions.explain: Lesson 30's build order avoids wasted rework: metrics first, then logs, then a basic trace, then the dashboard, with alerts last -- because alerts without a working dashboard to validate them against are just guesses.

questions.prompt: Select every deliverable the capstone expects by the end of Lesson 31, per Lesson 29's kickoff plan.
options: A running service with metrics, structured logs, and basic tracing
A dashboard with at least 4-6 meaningful panels
2-3 alert rules with real thresholds, not placeholders
A short write-up explaining your design decisions, ready to present as a portfolio piece
A load test proving the service handles at least 10x its normal traffic
questions.explain: By Lesson 31 the capstone expects a running instrumented service, a 4-6 panel dashboard, 2-3 real alert rules, and a short portfolio write-up. A load test to 10x traffic is never listed as a required deliverable -- at most it's mentioned as a possible 'what you'd do next' if you wanted to extend the project.
